actual_input_passages.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
actual_input_passages.text: If you have followed the previous rules, your notebooks should capture your entire process and be easy to read. But how will others access, run, and explore them? There are a number of ways you can support others’ reuse of your notebooks. First, store your notebooks in a public code repository with a clear README file and a liberal open source license ( https://opensource.org/licenses ) granting permission to reuse your code.

actual_input_passages.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
actual_input_passages.text: Read: Beyond granting permission to reuse your notebook, consider how you can leverage the unique structure of notebooks to support reading. At the very least, leave static HTML/PDF versions of all notebooks stored in the final version of the repository accompanying a publication. If, in 20 years, all other execution technology fails, these are likely to still provide a readable archival record, and with a full dependences list, future users are more likely to be able to recreate the compute environment. You can also use Nbviewer ( https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/ ) to provide static views of your executed notebook online without needing to convert it to a PDF/HTML document first. GitHub uses this service to render any notebooks on their site, so pushing a notebook to GitHub is another good way to make static views easily available. In both cases, you can point collaborators to a URL where they can read through your notebook online.

actual_input_passages.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
actual_input_passages.text: Run: To support others running your notebooks, you can use Binder [ 16 ] to provide a zero-install environment to run your notebooks in the cloud ( https://mybinder.org/ ). Binder enables community members to rerun your notebook online without needing to install Jupyter Notebook or Jupyter Lab on their own machine. More generally, you can create a portable containerized environment, for example, a Docker image ( https://docs.docker.com/ ), or create a dependency description file (see Rule 3 ) so future users of your notebook can more easily replicate your computing environment when rerunning your notebook.

blocks.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
blocks.text: If you have followed the previous rules, your notebooks should capture your entire process and be easy to read. But how will others access, run, and explore them? There are a number of ways you can support others’ reuse of your notebooks. First, store your notebooks in a public code repository with a clear README file and a liberal open source license ( https://opensource.org/licenses ) granting permission to reuse your code.

blocks.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
blocks.text: Read: Beyond granting permission to reuse your notebook, consider how you can leverage the unique structure of notebooks to support reading. At the very least, leave static HTML/PDF versions of all notebooks stored in the final version of the repository accompanying a publication. If, in 20 years, all other execution technology fails, these are likely to still provide a readable archival record, and with a full dependences list, future users are more likely to be able to recreate the compute environment. You can also use Nbviewer ( https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/ ) to provide static views of your executed notebook online without needing to convert it to a PDF/HTML document first. GitHub uses this service to render any notebooks on their site, so pushing a notebook to GitHub is another good way to make static views easily available. In both cases, you can point collaborators to a URL where they can read through your notebook online.

More generally, you can create a portable containerized environment, for example, a Docker image ( https://docs.docker.com/ ), or create a dependency description file (see Rule 3 ) so future users of your notebook can more easily replicate your computing environment when rerunning your notebook.

actual_input_passages.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
actual_input_passages.text: If you have followed the previous rules, your notebooks should capture your entire process and be easy to read. But how will others access, run, and explore them? There are a number of ways you can support others’ reuse of your notebooks. First, store your notebooks in a public code repository with a clear README file and a liberal open source license ( https://opensource.org/licenses ) granting permission to reuse your code.

actual_input_passages.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
actual_input_passages.text: Read: Beyond granting permission to reuse your notebook, consider how you can leverage the unique structure of notebooks to support reading. At the very least, leave static HTML/PDF versions of all notebooks stored in the final version of the repository accompanying a publication. If, in 20 years, all other execution technology fails, these are likely to still provide a readable archival record, and with a full dependences list, future users are more likely to be able to recreate the compute environment. You can also use Nbviewer ( https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/ ) to provide static views of your executed notebook online without needing to convert it to a PDF/HTML document first. GitHub uses this service to render any notebooks on their site, so pushing a notebook to GitHub is another good way to make static views easily available. In both cases, you can point collaborators to a URL where they can read through your notebook online.

baseline_blocks.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
baseline_blocks.text: If you have followed the previous rules, your notebooks should capture your entire process and be easy to read. But how will others access, run, and explore them? There are a number of ways you can support others’ reuse of your notebooks. First, store your notebooks in a public code repository with a clear README file and a liberal open source license ( https://opensource.org/licenses ) granting permission to reuse your code.

baseline_blocks.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
baseline_blocks.text: Read: Beyond granting permission to reuse your notebook, consider how you can leverage the unique structure of notebooks to support reading. At the very least, leave static HTML/PDF versions of all notebooks stored in the final version of the repository accompanying a publication. If, in 20 years, all other execution technology fails, these are likely to still provide a readable archival record, and with a full dependences list, future users are more likely to be able to recreate the compute environment. You can also use Nbviewer ( https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/ ) to provide static views of your executed notebook online without needing to convert it to a PDF/HTML document first. GitHub uses this service to render any notebooks on their site, so pushing a notebook to GitHub is another good way to make static views easily available. In both cases, you can point collaborators to a URL where they can read through your notebook online.

improved_blocks.heading: Rule 9: Design your notebooks to be read, run, and explored
improved_blocks.text: Run: To support others running your notebooks, you can use Binder [ 16 ] to provide a zero-install environment to run your notebooks in the cloud ( https://mybinder.org/ ). Binder enables community members to rerun your notebook online without needing to install Jupyter Notebook or Jupyter Lab on their own machine. More generally, you can create a portable containerized environment, for example, a Docker image ( https://docs.docker.com/ ), or create a dependency description file (see Rule 3 ) so future users of your notebook can more easily replicate your computing environment when rerunning your notebook.
